summary: Rand's comments on the socket conventions of RFC 167. It agrees with the conclusion that a major NCP overhaul is needed, but disagrees about the socket length. Because of limited storage in the TIP, Rand will assign sockets with the high-order 16 bits zero.

eli5.summary: A group says they like the new mailbox plan but the numbers are too long for their small machines. They will use shorter ones.

subtitle: Rand's concerns about socket address space requirements.

tldr.problem: RFC 167 proposed socket conventions for NCP communication, but Rand Corporation disagreed with the socket size requirements.
tldr.mechanism: Rand suggested using shorter socket numbers with high-order 16 bits set to zero, matching the constraints of their Terminal IMP (TIP) which had limited storage.
tldr.outcome: Rand proceeded with their own socket naming scheme compatible with UCSB and UCLA conventions, using the smaller address space they needed.

today: RFC 175 demonstrates an early ARPANET constraint: different sites had different hardware capabilities. Rand's pragmatic solution, aligning with peer sites, became one of several socket naming conventions used in the early network before standards fully converged.

sections.title: Socket Convention Disagreement
sections.content:
RFC 175 presents comments from Rand Corporation on RFC 167, "Socket Conventions Reconsidered," which proposed updates to NCP socket numbering conventions. Rand agreed with the overall conclusion that a major NCP overhaul was necessary, but disagreed on one critical point: the required size of socket numbers.

The main issue was that RFC 167's proposed socket sizes would not fit within the memory constraints of Rand's Terminal IMP (TIP), a smaller network interface unit that had limited storage capacity.
sections.eli5: Rand agreed the network needed new mailbox numbers, but they said the new numbers would be too big for their small computers.

sections.title: Rand's Socket Naming Scheme
sections.content:
Because of the TIP storage constraints, Rand decided to use sockets with the high-order 16 bits set to zero. This reduced the address space but made sockets manageable within their hardware limitations.

Rand's socket scheme divided the 32-bit socket field into four segments: bits 0-15 contained the gender bit (distinguishing send and receive sides); bits 16-23 contained an administratively assigned field for fixed socket identification associated with specific programs; bits 24-30 contained either zero for initial contact (ICP) sockets or values dynamically assigned by the user program; and the high-order bit 31 was zero.

Notably, Rand observed that repeatability of socket names across connections was not necessary for regular user processes, only for initial contact sockets used to establish new connections.
sections.eli5: They kept one part of the number for deciding if it was sending or receiving, another part for program names, and used the rest for temporary numbers they made up.

sections.title: Alignment with Other Sites
sections.content: Importantly, Rand noted that their socket naming scheme matched the conventions already adopted by UCSB and UCLA/CCN, creating consistency across three major network sites. This alignment meant that despite disagreeing with RFC 167, Rand could implement a solution that was compatible with other ARPANET sites working on similar constraints.
sections.eli5: Rand's shorter numbers worked the same way at other nearby universities, so they were all on the same page even though it was different from what RFC 167 said.
